It is item 238 of ul#search-list, the search box's type-ahead suggestion dropdown (class dropdown-menu): on the live page aui.css hides it (.aui .dropdown-menu{display:none}) and the inline filter() script shows it only after two or more characters are typed, and then only the items whose name contains the query. Rampa captured the page with the theme CSS unapplied (the screenshot is unstyled HTML, even the sr-only skip links show), so 1,628 of its 3,302 items appeared as an always-visible list of links. The 13 'Grupos de Pesquisa' links go to the research-group pages of different centers, departments and programs. All are different pages (live check). When the dropdown does show these items they look identical (same text, same chevron icon, no grouping or heading), so sighted users cannot tell them apart either. That is the 2.4.4 exception for purposes ambiguous to users in general: Understanding 2.4.4 says the person with a disability is not at a disadvantage when the page offers no context. ACT rule fd3a94 passes such pairs when there is no visual information that tells them apart, and it treats separate list items as different contexts. Different text for different destinations is only a best practice there.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is item 626 of ul#search-list, the search box's type-ahead suggestion dropdown: the text '(Poscivil) Graduate Program in Civil Engineering', linking to /poscivil. Neither the li nor the link has a lang attribute and the page is lang=pt-BR, so a screen reader would read the English words with Portuguese rules when the item is shown. On the live page the dropdown is hidden (.aui .dropdown-menu{display:none}) and shows this item only once a matching query such as 'civil' is typed; Rampa captured it unstyled, as always-visible text. The bigger doubt is the exception for proper names. The text is the program's own name (the /poscivil site is titled '(Poscivil) Graduate Program in Civil Engineering - UFPE'), and Understanding 3.1.2 says proper names generally need no change of language, naming specific entities 'including, but not limited to' brands, people and places. Against that, the text is a translated title made of ordinary English words. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether an English program name counts as a proper name, so I cannot call it either way.
